source_text:
καί μοι δοκῶ Λυδὸς ἐξαίφνης
εἶναι, τὰ Λυδῶν μιμησάμενος, οἳ τῷ ∆ιονύσῳ προσκείμενοι μόνον ἔαρ ἦγον ἡνίκα δὴ
καὶ τύχοι παρ' αὐτοῖς ὁ ∆ιόνυσος.
thought_title: Procopius likens himself to the Lydians
orientation: Procopius is praising the recipient's letter and now compares his own reaction to the Lydians' devotion to Dionysus.
pass_a_gloss: And I seem to myself suddenly to be a Lydian, having imitated the Lydians, who, devoted to Dionysus, observed spring only when Dionysus happened to be present among them.

choices.why: ἄγω with a season means to celebrate or observe it; 'observed' keeps the ritual sense without importing a modern holiday term.
The participle indicates attachment or allegiance; 'devoted to' captures the religious devotion to Dionysus.

choices.english: only when Dionysus happened to be present among them
choices.why: ἡνίκα with δὴ καὶ and the optative τύχοι marks an indefinite temporal clause; 'only when... happened to be' preserves the contingency.
The adverb marks the abruptness of the self-comparison; 'suddenly' is the plain equivalent.

pass_b_english: And I suddenly think I have become a Lydian, imitating the Lydians, who were devoted to Dionysus and observed spring only when Dionysus happened to be present among them.

last_rejected.quote: think I have become a Lydian
last_rejected.source_quote: καί μοι δοκῶ Λυδὸς ἐξαίφνης εἶναι
last_rejected.why: δοκῶ means 'seem' not 'think'; ἐξαίφνης modifies the whole clause as 'suddenly', not 'have become'
last_rejected.fix: And I suddenly seem to be a Lydian
last_rejected.ruling: δοκῶ μοι commonly means 'I think'; ἐξαίφνης 'suddenly' with εἶναι naturally yields 'suddenly have become'. No meaning lost.
